Melendez A.lab_name: Meléndez Lab, Department of Biology, Queens College, City University of New York (New York, New York, USA)
Melendez A.role: Developmental geneticist at Queens College, CUNY, who showed as a postdoc in Beth Levine's lab that autophagy genes are needed for the long life of insulin-signalling mutant worms. Her lab studies autophagy in C. elegans development, from germline stem cells to meiosis
Melendez A.sub: Professor, Department of Biology, Queens College, CUNY · Director, Office of Undergraduate Research, Queens College (since 2023) · postdoc with Beth Levine and before that with Iva Greenwald, Columbia University · PhD in Biology, Columbia University (Daniel Kalderon lab) · BA, Princeton University
story: In 2003, working in Beth Levine's lab at Columbia University, Alicia Meléndez was first author of a Science paper (MEL2003) that tied autophagy, the cell's self-recycling system, to lifespan in an animal. The roundworm C. elegans lives much longer when its insulin-like signalling is turned down by mutations in the receptor gene daf-2. When bec-1, the worm version of the autophagy gene beclin 1, was switched off in these long-lived worms, they lost their extra lifespan. They also could not properly form dauer larvae, a tough resting stage that young worms enter when food is short.

Why does this matter for mTOR? mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is one of the main brakes on autophagy, and several ways of extending lifespan in animals, from eating less to taking rapamycin, switch autophagy on. This paper was among the first to show that autophagy is required for a genetic lifespan extension, not just present alongside it. The work was done in worms, so it shows a mechanism in one animal rather than an effect in people.

Meléndez did her undergraduate thesis with Eric Wieschaus at Princeton University and earned a PhD in Biology at Columbia University with Daniel Kalderon. She was a postdoc with Iva Greenwald at Columbia before moving to Levine's lab to study autophagy in worms. Her own lab at Queens College, City University of New York, studies the role of autophagy in C. elegans development, with a focus on germline stem cell proliferation and the accuracy of meiosis, the cell division that makes eggs and sperm. She is a Professor of Biology and since 2023 also directs the college's Office of Undergraduate Research.

highlights.MEL2003: First author: showed in long-lived daf-2 worms that losing the autophagy gene bec-1 removes the extra lifespan and blocks normal dauer formation.

Lebrun F.lab_name: Institut Jules Bordet, Université Libre de Bruxelles (Brussels, Belgium)
Lebrun F.role: Medical oncologist at the Institut Jules Bordet in Brussels and a co-author of the BOLERO-2 trial reports that brought the mTOR inhibitor everolimus into breast cancer care
Lebrun F.sub: Department of Medicine, later Department of Oncology, Institut Jules Bordet, Université Libre de Bruxelles (PubMed affiliations 2012–2022)
story: Fabienne Lebrun is a co-author of both main reports of BOLERO-2 in this Atlas. BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had kept growing despite an aromatase inhibitor, a type of hormone therapy (BAS2012, PIC2014). All the women took the hormone drug exemestane; half also took everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex. Resistance to hormone therapy in these cancers is linked to overactive mTOR signalling, and adding everolimus more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review in the first report). That result led to the approval of everolimus for this use. The final report (PIC2014) confirmed the gain in progression-free survival, but overall survival was not significantly longer: median 31.0 versus 26.6 months. The main side effect was mouth sores (stomatitis).

The trial matters for the mTOR story because it was the first large test showing that blocking mTORC1 helps patients with a common cancer. It also shows the limits: the drug delayed tumour growth by months but did not clearly lengthen life.

Lebrun's papers in PubMed place her at the Institut Jules Bordet, the cancer hospital of the Université Libre de Bruxelles, first in the Department of Medicine and later in the Department of Oncology. Her other work includes a 2015 analysis of which tumour gene changes predicted benefit from everolimus in BOLERO-2, a 2013 phase 1 trial of temozolomide plus lapatinib for brain metastases in HER2-positive breast cancer, a 2017 review of intravenous iron for anaemic cancer patients, and a 2022 report of a rare liver side effect of combined immunotherapy and targeted therapy in kidney cancer. Her current position could not be confirmed from an official page; the affiliation shown is the most recent one in PubMed (2022).

Anderson RM.lab_name: Division of Geriatrics, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Anderson RM.role: Biologist of aging at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies how calorie restriction reshapes metabolism, and senior author of the 2017 comparison of the two long-running rhesus monkey calorie restriction studies
Anderson RM.sub: Division of Geriatrics, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison · Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center, William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital, Madison · earlier: Department of Pathology, Harvard Medical School (David Sinclair's group, papers 2002–2003)
story: Rozalyn Anderson was senior author of a 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that resolved an apparent conflict between two of the longest experiments in aging research. One group at the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin had followed rhesus monkeys on calorie restriction, eating less without malnutrition, for decades. Wisconsin had reported longer survival and the NIA had not. Analysing both studies side by side, the paper found consistent health benefits in both, and showed that the survival effect depended on study design and on what the control monkeys were fed.

Calorie restriction is the oldest known way to slow aging in animals, and lower mTORC1 activity is one of the routes through which it is thought to work. Monkeys are much closer to humans than mice are, so this comparison is among the strongest primate evidence that eating less improves health. It leaves open how large any lifespan gain would be.

Anderson worked on calorie restriction in yeast in David Sinclair's group at Harvard Medical School. In 2003 she was first author of papers in Nature and Science showing that the enzyme PNC1, which removes nicotinamide, is needed for calorie restriction to extend yeast lifespan, and that this effect does not depend on swings in the cell's NAD+ to NADH ratio. At the University of Wisconsin-Madison she is in the Division of Geriatrics of the Department of Medicine and the Geriatric Research, Education and Clinical Center of the Madison VA hospital. Her recent papers cover how calorie restriction remodels the mouse brain, how an acetyl-CoA transporter in the endoplasmic reticulum changes neuron metabolism, and sex differences in aging.

highlights.MAT2017: Senior author: led the joint analysis of the NIA and Wisconsin monkey studies, which found consistent health benefits of calorie restriction and a survival effect that depended on study design.

Baar EL.lab_name: Lamming Lab, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Baar EL.role: Researcher in Dudley Lamming's group at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who mapped how mTOR signalling changes with age in different mouse tissues and helped test gentler rapamycin dosing schedules
Baar EL.sub: Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison, and William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital (Lamming lab, papers 2014–2020, at the time of the study)
story: Emma Baar is a co-author of two linked mouse studies from Dudley Lamming's lab in this Atlas (ARR2015, ARR2016). Rapamycin is the best-tested drug for extending lifespan in mice, but given every day it causes side effects such as poor blood sugar control and weaker immune responses. In ARR2015, mice given rapamycin daily (2 mg/kg) became glucose intolerant and their insulin-producing islets released less insulin. The same dose given once every five days left glucose and insulin tolerance normal, while dosing every three days was already too frequent. In ARR2016, female mice that started the every-five-days schedule at 20 months of age, which is old for a mouse, lived longer than untreated females. Taken together, the two mouse studies suggest that rapamycin's lifespan benefit can be partly separated from its side effects by giving it intermittently. This conclusion comes from combining two experiments in mice, not from a single study, and has not been tested this way in people.

Baar was first author of a 2015 Aging Cell paper that measured mTOR signalling in several tissues of male and female mice at different ages and found that the changes with age differ by sex and by tissue. As a member of the Lamming group, Baar also co-authored work showing that losing Rictor, a core part of the second mTOR complex mTORC2, shortens the life of male mice (2014), that eating fewer branched-chain amino acids improves metabolic health (2016), that a new rapamycin-like drug can block mTORC1 selectively in animals (2019), and that the better insulin sensitivity seen with calorie restriction depends on mTORC2 in fat tissue (2019).
The most recent paper in PubMed with Baar's name is from 2020. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

highlights.ARR2015: Co-author: helped show that rapamycin given once every five days avoids the glucose intolerance seen with daily dosing in mice.
highlights.ARR2016: Co-author: helped show that the same every-five-days schedule, started at 20 months of age, extended the lifespan of female mice.

Babygirija R.lab_name: Lamming Lab, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Babygirija R.role: Researcher in Dudley Lamming's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies how restricting single amino acids in the diet affects metabolism, memory and Alzheimer's disease in mice
Babygirija R.sub: Graduate Program in Cellular and Molecular Biology and Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Lamming lab, papers from 2022) · earlier: Department of Surgery and Department of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Medical College of Wisconsin, and Aurora Research Institute, Milwaukee (papers 2012–2021)
story: Reji Babygirija was first author of a 2026 Advanced Science paper in this Atlas (BAB2025), first posted as a preprint. Branched-chain amino acids, leucine, isoleucine and valine, are building blocks of protein, and they act differently on mTORC1, the growth-control complex: leucine is a strong activator. The study restricted each of the three separately in 3xTg mice, a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The effects on memory and Alzheimer's-type brain changes were distinct for each amino acid and differed between males and females. Cutting isoleucine or valine, but not leucine, improved metabolic health. The results come from mice and point to diet composition, not just total protein, as something that matters.

Before joining Lamming's group, Babygirija worked at the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. As first author of a 2012 Brain Research paper from Takahashi's group in the Department of Surgery, Babygirija showed in rats that social interaction softened stress responses after chronic stress in animals separated from their mothers early in life. Later papers from Milwaukee covered visceral pain after bladder inflammation in young rats (2017), irritable bowel symptoms in inflammatory bowel disease (2019) and electro-acupuncture against chronic stress (2021).

At the University of Wisconsin-Madison, in the graduate program in cellular and molecular biology, Babygirija has co-authored many of the Lamming lab's diet studies, including a 2022 Cell Metabolism paper showing that sex and genetic background shape how mice respond to protein restriction. PubMed lists more than 60 papers with the name.

highlights.BAB2025: First author: restricted each branched-chain amino acid separately in Alzheimer's model mice and found distinct, sex-specific effects, with isoleucine and valine restriction improving metabolic health.

Knopf BA.lab_name: Lamming Lab, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Knopf BA.role: Researcher in Dudley Lamming's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and first author of a 2026 review that sets out the hallmarks of protein and amino acid restriction in aging
Knopf BA.sub: Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison, and William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital (Lamming lab, papers from 2025)
story: Bailey Knopf was first author of a 2026 review in Cell Press Blue (KNO2026) that asks what eating less protein does to an aging body. Across many organisms, cutting dietary protein, or only certain essential amino acids such as methionine, isoleucine and valine, improves metabolic health and can lengthen healthy life and lifespan. The review argues that the make-up of the protein, which amino acids it contains, matters as much as the amount, and that much of the effect runs through nutrient-sensing pathways, including mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Most of the evidence it summarises comes from animals.

Knopf is also a co-author of the Lamming lab's 2026 study on restricting single branched-chain amino acids in Alzheimer's model mice (BAB2025), in which cutting isoleucine or valine, but not leucine, improved metabolic health. PubMed lists about a dozen papers with Knopf's name since 2025, all from Lamming's group, including a 2025 preprint showing that the body's production of ketone bodies is not needed for the metabolic changes caused by calorie restriction in mice. No position beyond the Lamming lab could be confirmed.

highlights.KNO2026: First author of this review defining the hallmarks of protein and amino acid restriction in aging.
highlights.BAB2025: Co-author of the study restricting single branched-chain amino acids in Alzheimer's model mice.

story: Adriana Benavides is a co-author of KRA2018, a small trial in San Antonio that asked a basic question before any longevity trial: is daily rapamycin safe for healthy older people? In this randomised pilot trial, 25 people aged 70 to 95 were followed for eight weeks or more. The drug was well tolerated, with only minor changes in red blood cells, and in this short window it did not raise blood glucose or cause insulin resistance, a side effect seen with daily rapamycin in mice. The trial was too small and too short to measure any effect on aging itself, but it laid groundwork for larger studies such as PEARL.

PubMed links Benavides to rapamycin and immune research in San Antonio and Philadelphia. Benavides co-authored a 2012 Aging Cell study from San Antonio showing that lifelong rapamycin improved age-related memory problems in mice, a 2015 review on how invariant natural killer T cells, a type of immune cell, attack tumours (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia), and a 2016 paper on how mice adapt to long-term rapamycin, which lists both institutions. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.KRA2018: Co-author of this pilot trial, which tracked immune, metabolic and other safety measures in older adults taking rapamycin.

Ullern H.lab_name: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, University of Oslo (Oslo, Norway)
Ullern H.role: Researcher in Helene Knævelsrud's autophagy group at the University of Oslo and first author of a 2026 study of folliculin loss in Birt-Hogg-Dubé kidney cancer
Ullern H.sub: Department of Molecular Medicine, Institute of Basic Medical Sciences, and Centre for Cancer Cell Reprogramming, University of Oslo (papers 2025–2026)
story: Halvor Ullern was first author of a 2026 Autophagy Reports paper in this Atlas (ULL2026). Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome is an inherited condition in which people carry a faulty copy of the FLCN gene and can develop kidney tumours. Folliculin, the FLCN protein, is part of the switch that controls mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomes and autophagy. In kidney cancer cells from patients, losing FLCN kept TFEB permanently in the nucleus and made mTORC1 overactive. Bulk autophagy, the cell's self-recycling, still ran normally. Even so, the autophagy receptor p62 (SQSTM1) piled up in enlarged clumps, and the same build-up was seen in kidney tumours from a Norwegian group of patients.

The lesson for researchers is practical: a build-up of p62 is often read as a sign that autophagy is blocked, but here it was not. The study used patient-derived cells and tumour samples, so it describes this one cancer type.

Ullern works in Helene Knævelsrud's group in the Department of Molecular Medicine at the University of Oslo. In 2025 Ullern was also first author of a review in the Journal of Molecular Biology on the links between autophagy and sleep. PubMed lists two papers with the name; no further career details were found.

highlights.ULL2026: First author: showed in Birt-Hogg-Dubé kidney cancer cells and patient tumours that p62 accumulates even though bulk autophagy still works.

Sharp ZD.role: Molecular biologist at UT Health San Antonio who works on rapamycin and aging in mice, from the Interventions Testing Program lifespan studies to cancer prevention in tumour-prone mice
Sharp ZD.sub: Department of Molecular Medicine and Institute of Biotechnology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · Mays Cancer Center (PubMed affiliations to 2023)
story: Zelton Dave Sharp is a co-author of three Interventions Testing Program (ITP) papers in this Atlas. The ITP, funded by the US National Institute on Aging, tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites at once, so a result has to hold up in different labs. In HAR2009, rapamycin added to food from 600 days of age, already late in a mouse's life, extended both median and maximum lifespan in males and females. MIL2011 showed in the same design that rapamycin raised median lifespan by 10 to 18 percent while resveratrol and simvastatin had no effect. MIL2014 found that the gain depends on dose, is larger in females, and works differently from dietary restriction. These were the first convincing drug results for lifespan in mammals, but they are mouse results.

Sharp's own papers follow the same drug. As senior author, Sharp showed in 2013 that rapamycin lengthens the life of mice carrying one faulty copy of the Rb1 tumour suppressor gene by holding back their neuroendocrine tumours, and in 2016 described how mice adapt to long-term rapamycin. Sharp also co-authored a 2019 study linking mTORC1 to muscle fibre damage with age, and in 2023 was first author of a review in Experimental Gerontology calling rapamycin the only drug consistently shown to increase mammalian lifespan.

PubMed lists Sharp in the Department of Molecular Medicine and the Institute of Biotechnology at UT Health San Antonio, with links to the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies and the Mays Cancer Center.

highlights.MIL2011: Co-author: rapamycin extended lifespan in the same experiment in which resveratrol and simvastatin did not.
highlights.MIL2014: Co-author: the lifespan gain from rapamycin depends on dose, is larger in females and differs from dietary restriction.

Pledger ES.lab_name: Cate Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Pledger ES.role: Researcher in Jamie Cate's lab at UC Berkeley who used ribosome profiling to show that exhausted human T cells shut down a key class of growth-related mRNAs even while mTOR is active
Pledger ES.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley (Cate lab, papers 2025–2026)
story: Erica Pledger was first author of a 2026 RNA Biology paper in this Atlas (PLEDGER2026), first posted as a preprint in 2025. CD8+ T cells are the immune cells that kill infected and cancer cells. When they are stimulated for too long, for example inside a tumour, they become exhausted and stop working well. The team made human CD8+ T cells exhausted in the dish and used ribosome profiling, a method that shows which messenger RNAs are actually being read by ribosomes, to see what proteins the cells were making.

One group of messages stood out: 5' TOP mRNAs, which code for ribosome parts and other protein-making machinery. Their translation is normally switched on by mTORC1, the growth-control complex. In exhausted T cells these messages were strongly held back even though mTOR activity was high, which points to a second layer of control that overrides or bypasses mTOR. The work was done in cultured human cells, not in patients.

Pledger works in Jamie Cate's lab at UC Berkeley, which studies how ribosomes and the initiation factor eIF3 decide which mRNAs are made into protein. PubMed lists two papers with Pledger's name, the preprint and the published version.

highlights.PLEDGER2026: First author: showed by ribosome profiling that exhausted human CD8+ T cells repress 5' TOP mRNAs despite high mTOR activity.

Goul C.lab_name: Zoncu Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Goul C.role: Cell biologist in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley, first author of a major review of how mTORC1 senses nutrients and of a 2026 Nature study on how damaged lysosomes are repaired
Goul C.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Zoncu lab, papers 2022–2026)
story: Claire Goul was first author of a 2023 review in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology (GOU2023) that explains how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, senses nutrients. mTORC1 is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when amino acids, glucose, cholesterol and growth signals are all present, and it then drives the making of proteins, fats and new cell parts. The review walks through the sensors and switches involved, including the Rag GTPases that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome, and how faults in this system contribute to metabolic disease, cancer and other conditions. It is a good entry point for a reader who wants the whole pathway in one place.

Goul's research in Roberto Zoncu's lab centres on the lysosome. In 2022 Goul co-wrote a short Developmental Cell commentary on lysosome repair, and in 2026 was first author of a Nature paper describing LASER, which links the sensing of lysosome damage to the assembly of the ESCRT machinery that patches the membrane. Goul also co-authored a 2025 EMBO Journal study showing that autophagosomes anchor a checkpoint that shapes PKA signalling in neurons.
PubMed lists Goul at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at UC Berkeley on all papers from the Zoncu lab, 2022 to 2026.

highlights.GOU2023: First author of this review of how mTORC1 senses nutrients and signals in metabolism and disease.

Castellano BM.lab_name: Zoncu Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Castellano BM.role: Cell biologist who, in Roberto Zoncu's lab at UC Berkeley, showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome switches on mTORC1 through the SLC38A9 and NPC1 proteins
Castellano BM.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Zoncu lab, papers 2015–2017, at the time of the study)
story: Castellano was first author of a 2017 Science paper in this Atlas (CAS2017). Every cell has to decide whether it has enough raw materials to grow. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, makes that decision on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, where it is switched on when nutrients are present. Amino acids were the best-known signal; CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is another one. SLC38A9, a transporter-like protein already known to sense the amino acid arginine, is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and it uses separate cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein to do it. story: Daniel Nomura is a co-author of two papers from Roberto Zoncu's lab in this Atlas about cholesterol as a signal for growth. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when nutrients are present. story: Ming-Yuan Su was first author of SUX2017, a 2017 Molecular Cell paper from James Hurley's lab at UC Berkeley. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is recruited to the lysosome by the Rag GTPases, which sit on a scaffold called Ragulator. It is a protein-level study, which later work built on to explain how nutrients flip the Rag switch.

Su stayed with structures of lysosome-linked machines. As first author of a 2020 Nature paper, Su solved the cryo-EM structure of the C9orf72-SMCR8-WDR41 complex, which is reduced in some forms of ALS and frontotemporal dementia, and showed that it acts as a GTPase-activating protein for ARF proteins. Since 2021 PubMed lists Su in the Department of Biochemistry at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) in Shenzhen, as corresponding author. The group's cryo-EM work there includes structures of GATOR2 bound to the amino acid sensors CASTOR1 and Sestrin2 (2025), of the KICSTOR and GATOR1-KICSTOR complexes that anchor an mTORC1 brake on the lysosome (2025, with Chun-Yan Lim), and of ubiquitin ligase complexes such as DDB1-AMBRA1 (2023) and COP1-DET1 (2026).

story: Breanne Sparta was first author of a 2023 eLife paper in this Atlas (SPA2023). Most experiments on mTORC1, the growth-control complex, grind up millions of cells and measure an average at a few time points. This study filmed single living human breast epithelial cells (MCF10A) carrying fluorescent reporters, and followed TFEB, a regulator of lysosomes and autophagy that mTORC1 holds outside the nucleus, together with AMPK and AKT activity. mTORC1-TFEB signalling adjusted smoothly to amino acids and insulin whether they were given alone, one after the other or together. At normal body levels of amino acids the three signals rose and fell in step, and these graded changes tracked how fast the cells were making protein. The results come from one cultured cell line.

Sparta's earlier work in Albeck's lab also used live-cell reporters. As first author of a 2015 Journal of Biological Chemistry paper, Sparta showed that pulses of ERK activity triggered by the growth factor EGF depend on mechanisms at the receptor. Sparta co-authored a 2017 methods chapter on imaging ERK signalling with fluorescent biosensors, a 2017 modelling study of oscillations in MAPK signalling, and a 2021 Cell Metabolism paper on how single cells pass through temporary phases of resistance to drugs that block mitochondrial energy production. Sparta's current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.SPA2023: First author: used live single-cell imaging to show that mTORC1-TFEB signalling adjusts continuously to amino acids and insulin and tracks protein synthesis.
